name: Adropin
lead: Adropin is a 76-amino-acid peptide encoded by the ENHO gene, reported in 2008 in Cell Metabolism as a secreted factor linking dietary macronutrient intake with energy homeostasis and lipid metabolism in mice.[1][2] Its name derives from Latin words for 'set fire to' and 'fat'.[2]

It is made mainly in the liver and brain. Animal studies report effects on glucose tolerance, fat use, endothelial function and physical activity, while human data consist mostly of blood-level associations with obesity, ageing and cardiometabolic disease.[3][4][5][6]
Adropin is an endogenous peptide. The sources reviewed describe no approved therapeutic use.

paras: The peptide is highly conserved across mammals and is expressed most strongly in the brain, as well as in the liver, heart and gut. Liver expression follows feeding status.[2]

Mice lacking adropin showed increased adiposity and insulin resistance.[3] Treatment improved glucose tolerance and substrate use in diet-induced obese mice.[4] A separate mouse study reported a role in physical activity via NB-3/Notch signalling,[5] and another reported effects on endothelial function.[6]

Low circulating adropin has been reported with obesity and ageing, and levels were reported to rise after gastric bypass surgery.[7] Low serum adropin has also been associated with coronary atherosclerosis.[8] These are associations and do not establish cause.

No studies found testing adropin as a treatment for appearance or body composition. Registered human studies are observational, measuring serum adropin in conditions such as chronic liver disease, periodontal disease and obesity.[9][10]

card.summary: A liver and brain peptide linked to fat metabolism in mice; human data are blood-level associations only.
card.note: Endogenous peptide; no approved use or human treatment trials found.

quick.overview:
Adropin is a small peptide made mostly in the liver and brain. In mice, low levels go with more body fat and insulin resistance, and giving it improved glucose handling.

In people, lower blood levels have been associated with obesity and heart disease, but no trials test adropin as a way to change body fat or appearance.
quick.mechanism: It is cleaved from the ENHO gene product, and its expression follows feeding and the body clock. The receptor is not fully established; GPR19 has been proposed.
quick.risks: No approved product exists and the sources reviewed give no human safety data for administering it.
